for the shape it can see everywhere in git history and .endless/LESSONS.md:
`tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh`, the path E-2023 retired.

`.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md` states the rules, but a directory-level CLAUDE.md
only reaches a session already working in that directory — which is exactly
what these sessions fail to do. The rules are in the room the session never
enters.

Observed repeatedly after E-2023 landed: sessions write the suite the old way,
and being told to fix it sends them into a long investigation of E-2023 rather
than a two-line correction.

## The change

One sentence appended to the `handoff_verify` partial, plus its render test:

    ... folding this task's own tests into that one suite as a fail-fast check.
    The suite goes at `.endless/tasks/e-NNNN/verify.sh` and sources
    `../_harness.sh` as its first statement; see `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.

It is a shared partial, so it reaches all ten handoffs (five spawn types x the
spawn and claim wrappers) at once — the E-1947/E-2073 pattern of editing the
partial rather than the wrappers.

## What it does not cover, and what does instead

Only NEWLY spawned sessions. A session already running was handed its text
before the change existed. For those, Mike runs a throwaway fixer that
relocates the suite, inserts the harness source, and rewrites the header,
printing a notice that tells the session what changed and explicitly not to
investigate it. That script is deliberately not product surface and is not part
of this task.

---

# Corrected mechanism (added 2026-08-31 by ES-1163 / E-1661, folding in E-2096)

Hit the same wall independently while finishing E-1661: every Write/Edit
refused, the work finished through a Bash heredoc, same gate. Filed as E-2096,
now marked a duplicate of this task. What the second sighting establishes is
that the trigger named above is not the real one.

`IdleSession` has exactly ONE caller: the Stop hook, internal/hookcmd/claude.go
:375. Nothing on the `task update --status unverified` path idles a session,
and nothing in the turn loop writes 'working' back — TouchSession's ON CONFLICT
UPDATE preserves the existing state by design (internal/monitor/session.go:346;
that CASE revives only an 'ended' row). The only writers of state='working' are
BindSessionToTask (claim/bind) and StartChatSession.

So the trigger is ANY Stop that reaches IdleSession — not reporting unverified,
and not E-2096's own guess (a turn started from a `!` bash-input, which fires no
UserPromptSubmit). Neither a prompt nor a bash-input restores 'working': a
session that ends one turn cleanly is already stranded. The correlation with
unverified is that reporting it tends to be the last thing a session does before
a clean Stop.

Residual the claim-path seam does not reach. In the E-1661 sighting `task claim`
never got as far as the "you already hold this" early return — it refused first
with "E-1661 is in status 'unverified'; re-claiming would demote it to
'underway'". Treating --force as the answer for the settled-status half means
the only route back to 'working' for a task past `underway` demotes that task to
repair a session field. Whatever lands here should reactivate without that side
effect.

None of this disturbs the two rejected shapes: idle is still meaningful, and a
gate that accepts idle is still a hole.

fields.outcome: Duplicate of E-2093's first item — same gate, same stranded 'idle' session, same Bash-heredoc workaround. Investigation folded into E-2093's analysis, including the correction that the trigger is any Stop reaching IdleSession (not reporting unverified, and not this task's own guess about bash-input), and the residual that a task past 'underway' has no non-demoting route back to 'working'.

payload.title: Bracket an agent's CLI refusal with a repeated one-line verdict so a truncating pipe keeps it
payload.description: A refusal's verdict is line 2 of 17; an agent that pipes through tail -3 keeps lines 15-17 and never sees it. Measured on task add/update: five refusals across two verbs, one answered by shaving 34 characters off a title without ever reading the 107>100 the error stated twice, and one by writing a junk value to a live record to probe the validator. Fix: when agent_env.present(), emit ONE dense verdict line as both the FIRST and LAST line of the refusal, with the existing guidance unchanged between them. Identical lines, not split, so whichever end survives a truncation is sufficient on its own. Humans see today's message unchanged - the duplication is agent-only by design.
payload.text:
# Plan — Bracket an agent's CLI refusal with a repeated one-line verdict

## The failure this fixes, measured

`endless task update E-2093 --title <104 chars>` refuses with 17 lines on
stderr. The verdict is line 2:

    1
    2   Error: Title is 104 characters; max is 100.
    3
    4-16  (fourteen lines of guidance on how to shape a title)
    17

An agent piping `2>&1 | tail -3` keeps lines 15-17 — the tail of the guidance
block. The one line that names the constraint is the one line a small window
cannot see.

What that cost, in one session, across `task add` and `task update` (both call
`validate_title`, task_cmd.py:312, from :2252 and :4624):

1. `task add`, title 107 chars — refused. Read the fragment as a SHAPE
   complaint, reworded, and passed at 94 by accident while believing the shape
   was the problem.
2. `task add`, description 1032 > 1024 — refused.
3. `task update --title`, 141 chars — refused.
4. `task update --title`, 107 chars — refused. Thirty-four characters shaved
   between attempts 3 and 4 without ever reading the number the error stated
   both times. That is editing toward a constraint rather than reading it.
5. `--title "test"` written to a LIVE task to probe the validator — a mutation
   of real state to learn what the error had already said twice.
6. `--description-file` with newlines — refused.

Five refusals and one junk write, all against a message that was correct,
complete, and on stderr the whole time.

## The change

When `agent_env.present()` (src/endless/agent_env.py:116 — the same signal
`internal/agentenv` uses; NOT the `--agent-view` flag, because an agent will
never pass a flag it does not know it needs), a refusal is emitted as:

    <verdict line>
    <blank>
    … today's guidance block, unchanged …
    <blank>
    <verdict line>          ← byte-identical to the first

The two lines are IDENTICAL, deliberately. Split them — verdict first, remedy
last — and `head -N` yields the problem without the fix while `tail -N` yields
the fix without the problem. Identical means whichever end survives is
sufficient alone, and seeing both reads as one repeat rather than two findings.

Length is unconstrained: `head`/`tail` are line-based, so a 200-character line
survives whole. Keep it to one dense line rather than a paragraph — a paragraph
invites the same skimming that caused this.

## What the verdict line must carry

Ordered by what would have stopped the failure above at attempt 3:

1. **Measured numbers, never an adjective.** `title 107>100 chars`, not "too
   long". The number is what makes the correction computable.
2. **A fixed sentinel plus the command and field**: `ENDLESS-ERROR task add:`.
   A bare error line read out of context does not say what produced it.
3. **Where the overflow goes**, not merely "shorten": `long-form goes in
   --analysis (rationale) or --text (plan); the title names WHAT`. Without
   this an agent mangles the field to fit instead of relocating the content —
   which is what happened.
4. **Whether anything changed**: `Nothing was created.` A refusal leaves an
   agent wondering whether it partially applied; that uncertainty is part of
   what produced the junk write in step 5.
5. **Every problem at once**, not the first. See below.

Deliberately NOT in it: the template, the HOW-vs-WHAT rationale, the examples.
Those are worth having and worth losing.

Not JSON, not key=value. A stable prefix and a plain sentence parses fine and
stays readable when a human hits it.

Worked example, ~170 characters:

    ENDLESS-ERROR task add: title 107>100 chars; description 1032>1024 chars. Long-form goes in --analysis (rationale) or --text (plan); the title names WHAT. Nothing was created.

## Collect every problem before refusing

Today `validate_title` raises on the first failure, so the sequence is: fix the
title, resubmit, discover the description. Steps 1-2 and 3-6 above are both
that shape. The validators for title, description and analysis on `task add`
and `task update` should accumulate their findings and refuse once, with all of
them in the verdict line.

Scope this to those validators on those two verbs. It is not a project-wide
refactor of every ClickException.

## Shape it as a shared helper

A rule that reaches two messages is not a convention. Add one helper — e.g.
`agent_error(summary: str, guidance: str)` beside the existing agent-facing
machinery — that renders the bracketed form when `agent_env.present()` and
today's plain form otherwise. Adopt it first in the title/description
validators, and document it so a new refusal reaches for it.

## Humans see no change

The duplication is agent-only. A person reading the full message in a terminal
gets today's output byte for byte. This is a requirement, not a nicety: a
repeated long line is noise to a reader who was never going to truncate it.

## Boundaries

- Does NOT touch which stream errors go to. They are already on stderr, already
  complete; the agent truncated them. Nothing about stdout/stderr changes.
- Does NOT add a PreToolUse matcher against `2>&1 | tail`. That was considered
  and rejected: it targets a correlate, would not catch `| tail -N` over a long
  stdout report, and would fire on `go test ./... 2>&1 | tail -30`, which is
  correct usage (a failing `go test` writes to stdout; a failing `endless`
  leaves stdout empty — measured).
- Does NOT reorder the existing guidance. The bracket makes order irrelevant.

## PRODUCT

Nothing here is Endless-specific. Every project using Endless is driven by
agents that pipe and truncate CLI output, and every CLI puts its verdict first
and its teaching after. The agent-gated bracket belongs in the shipped CLI, and
the detection signal (`agent_env.present()`) already ships.

## Verify — .endless/tasks/e-<id>/verify.sh

1. Fail-fast unit gate: the Python tests this task adds.
2. Under a simulated agent env, a refusal's first and last lines are
   byte-identical.
3. That line carries the measured numbers, the command, the field, the
   destination for long-form content, and the no-change statement.
4. `… 2>&1 | tail -3` and `… 2>&1 | head -3` of the same refusal EACH contain
   the verdict — the two ends of the property.
5. With no agent env, the message is byte-identical to today's: no duplication,
   no sentinel.
6. A call that violates title AND description limits at once names both in one
   verdict line and refuses once.
7. A refused call mutated nothing.

fields.description: Repointed: the test is not where this belongs. E-2023's runner hands every suite a temp HOME from os.MkdirTemp, and on macOS the OS temp root sits beneath a symlinked prefix (var -> private/var) — so every suite runs under a HOME reached through a symlink, which a real home directory almost never is. That is an artifact of the isolation MECHANISM, not a property of the code under test; it is platform-dependent (passes on Linux, fails on macOS); and it makes suites fail for reasons unrelated to their own task, which is the one thing a verification front door must never do. Fix: canonicalize the run dir in makeRunDir with filepath.EvalSymlinks. One line. The whole internal/monitor package then passes under a temp HOME, so the planned per-test fix and the sweep for other HOME-sensitive tests both become unnecessary.

fields.title: Canonicalize the verify runner's temp HOME so suites stop failing on a symlinked macOS temp root

fields.analysis:
Repointed 2026-08-31 by ES-1159 (E-2023), at Mike's direction, after he asked
whether E-2023 could have been implemented so that this task were unnecessary.
It could — and the answer moves the fix from the test to the runner.

## What was originally filed, and why it was the wrong layer

`TestProjectPath_TildeExpandsToHome` (internal/monitor/projects_test.go) builds
its expectation as `filepath.Join(os.UserHomeDir(), "some-project")` and
compares it against `ProjectPath`, which returns the RESOLVED form. The two
agree only when HOME is not itself reached through a symlink. The original plan
was to fix the expectation and sweep for the same shape elsewhere.

The test IS wrong — it compares a resolved value against an unresolved one. But
nothing had ever observed it, and after the change below nothing will again.
Under ED-1550, "noticing something true does not earn a task."

## Where it actually belongs

`makeRunDir` (internal/verifycmd/env.go) takes `os.MkdirTemp("")` verbatim. On
macOS that lands beneath a symlinked prefix, so the runner hands every suite a
HOME reached through a symlink — something a real home directory almost never
is.

Three reasons that is the runner's bug and not the test's:

1. It is an artifact of the isolation MECHANISM, not a property of the system
   under test. The runner's job is to substitute HOME transparently; anything
   else it changes is noise it injected.
2. It is platform-dependent. The same suite, the same code, passes on Linux
   (the temp root is not symlinked there) and fails on macOS. A runner whose
   verdict depends on the OS's mktemp implementation emits false signal.
3. It misattributes failures — this task's own sharpest observation, that "the
   failure it reports will point at the wrong task." That is precisely the harm
   E-2023 exists to prevent.

The counter-argument from E-2023's plan — "a break is a finding, not a
regression" — was written about suites that secretly depended on the real
database, where the dependency was always a contract violation. It does not
transfer. Nothing in the contract says a suite must tolerate a symlinked HOME,
and the runner is not a fuzzer; a deliberate test of symlinked-HOME behaviour is
a thing someone can write on purpose.

## The change

`filepath.EvalSymlinks` on the freshly created temp dir, failing open (a
directory this process just made should always resolve; if it does not, running
under the unresolved path beats refusing to verify).

Measured before and after:

    raw temp HOME       -> FAIL  ProjectPath = "<resolved>" want "<unresolved>"
    resolved temp HOME  -> ok    internal/monitor

The whole `internal/monitor` package passes under a resolved temp HOME, with
that test the only failure under the raw one — so the sweep this task planned
finds nothing left to fix.

## Pinned, not left to the platform

Three tests, because the invariant is invisible on Linux and would rot silently:

- `TestMakeRunDir_IsCanonical` — the run dir equals its EvalSymlinks form.
- `TestIsolatedEnv_HomeIsCanonical` — HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME, the values
  consumers actually see, are canonical.
- `TestRun_ScriptSuite_SeesCanonicalHome` — end to end through the real runner:
  a suite observing a non-canonical HOME exits 30 and fails the test.

## Verification of the original symptom, end to end

A throwaway suite driven through `endless-go verify`, whose check was the exact
repro from the original filing, printed a canonical HOME and passed. Before the
change it failed.

## PRODUCT

Nothing macOS-specific in the fix, though the symptom is. Any platform whose
temp root is symlinked hands the same trap to every downstream project's
suites, and the runner is shipped surface.

fields.text:
# Plan — E-2023: one front door for verify suites

Governed by ED-1534 (verify suites are land-time tests; mass-porting them to
`verify.toml` is not pragmatic). Complementary to E-1916, which enforces the same
rule at the PreToolUse hook; this task enforces it at the runner, where the task
id is known for certain rather than parsed out of a command string.

## What this task became, and why

Filed as "add a guard inside each script". That is no longer the shape. Three
things moved:

- **A runner already exists and already isolates.** `endless task verify <id>`
  runs a per-run temp `HOME` + `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (internal/verifycmd/env.go).
  Because Go's `PinMainDB` resolves through `os.UserHomeDir`, even a script that
  drives the hook binary writes into the temp home rather than the real database.
  That is containment an in-script guard cannot provide.
- **The runner knows the id.** Own-task-only becomes structural. A command-string
  predicate cannot extract an id from a glob loop over the script directory, and
  that exact shape is what caused the E-2071 incident.
- **ED-1534 forbids the bulk retrofit** an in-script guard would have required
  across ~200 landed scripts — which the guide separately forbids editing.

The rule is unchanged. The enforcement point moved from 200 places to one.

## 1. Move the scripts beside the manifests

`tests/tasks/e-<id>-verify.sh` becomes `.endless/tasks/e-<id>/verify.sh`.

Two reasons, and the second is why this belongs in THIS task rather than a later
one:

- `tests/` is too strong a signal. It reads as a suite you maintain and re-run,
  which is what makes `just test`, a glob, or "run the tests before handing off"
  reach them. A land-time artifact does not belong beside a regression suite.
- One directory per task, holding whichever form that task uses. `verify.Discover`
  already walks `.endless/tasks/<id>/`, so the script fallback below becomes
  "same directory, other filename" instead of a second search path — and a task
  that later grows a manifest keeps its script beside it rather than across the
  repo.

`git mv` per script so history follows. Directory ids are lowercase by
convention but `verify.NormalizeTaskID` already compares normalized, so either
casing resolves — do not add a second casing rule here.

`_harness.sh` (section 3) lands at `.endless/tasks/_harness.sh`. Discovery
iterates directory entries looking for per-task dirs, so a plain file alongside
them is skipped; add a test pinning that rather than relying on it.

Update the live references: the guide, the justfile, and the pytest files that
name the old path.

E-1916's plan carries a predicate table naming the old path. It is not amended
here — a plan records what was true when it was written, and rewriting another
task's plan to match work that has not landed puts a claim in it that nothing
verifies. Whichever of the two lands second reconciles against the tree it finds.
Worth knowing when E-1916 is picked up: this move SIMPLIFIES it, because both
suite forms end up under the single `.endless/tasks/<id>/` segment its predicate
already keys on. Its carve-out for `.endless/verify.toml` at the project root is
unaffected.

## 2. The runner falls back to the script

`internal/verifycmd.run` currently fails when `verify.Discover` finds no manifest:

    endless-go verify: no verification suite found for task

Add a fallback ahead of that error: if the task's directory holds `verify.sh`,
run it as a single raw check under the same isolation the manifest path uses, and
normalize its output the same way. Only when the directory holds neither does the
error stand — naming both filenames it looked for.

Both filenames are product-controlled constants beside `verify.SuitesDir`, not
literals at the call site, so a downstream project laying suites out differently
is a config change rather than a fork.

## 3. The refusal, and the marker

Before running anything, refuse when the requested task is **landed AND is not
this session's active task** — E-1916's predicate exactly, reusing the same
`session-query task-report --id N` `landed` bool rather than inventing a second
notion of landed-ness. One rule, two enforcement points, no divergence: a session
must never get different answers from `just verify` and the hook.

Bare `endless task verify` with no id resolves to the session's own active task
(src/endless/verify_cmd.py already does this) and is always allowed — that is the
pre-land gate doing its job.

**A task may always verify itself again, landed or not.** The conjunction is what
makes this work: a task that landed and was then reopened is the claiming
session's ACTIVE task, so `not active` is false and the refusal does not fire.
Re-verifying and re-landing your own reopened work is the documented path when
shipped work turns out wrong (`endless guide orchestration`: "Re-verify with the
suite that already exists"), and E-2071 exercised exactly that — landed, reopened
to `revisit`, extended, landed again. Nothing here may narrow that. A predicate
keyed on landed-ness ALONE would break it, which is the reason for the second
conjunct, not an incidental detail of E-1916's wording.

The refusal names what to do instead rather than only saying no, and says why a
landed suite's result is meaningless (ED-1534: its fixtures were pinned to that
task's moment).

Then, absorbed from E-1623's half 1 (declined in favour of this task):

- Extract the duplicated `report_*`/`assert_*`/`section`/`summary` block into
  `_harness.sh`, emitting TAP so a sourcing script's assertions are normalizable
  with no rewrite. This is E-1623's design, unchanged.
- The runner exports a marker into the suite's environment. `_harness.sh` refuses
  when the marker is absent, so running a script directly exits non-zero with a
  message naming `just verify E-<id>`.
- The marker is set by the runner only. It is NOT documented as a user-settable
  escape: an override an agent can set is an override an agent can rationalize,
  which is the failure this task exists to stop.

Per ED-1534 the existing scripts are NOT bulk-retrofitted to source the lib. New
scripts source it, plus a few converted exemplars to prove it. **Stated
limitation:** a script that does not source the lib stays directly runnable, and
for those the only guard is E-1916's hook. That is a deliberate boundary, not an
oversight — recorded so nobody reads "refused unless run through the runner" as
universal.

## 4. `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md` — the reasoning, at the point of contact

A directory-level CLAUDE.md stating the rules for suites in that tree: land-time
gate not regression suite, do not run another task's, do not edit a landed one,
bit-rot is expected (ED-1534), coverage that must survive belongs in the
project's own suite, and `just verify E-<id>` is how you run one.

Its job is to be the explanation the refusal points at — an agent working in that
directory meets the reasoning before it acts, instead of having to go find it in
`endless guide orchestration`. Refusals in section 3 should reference it by path
so the "why" is one read away from the "no".

**It ships with every project.** `register_project` (behind both `project init`
and `project register`) already scaffolds `.gitignore`, `.endless/tmp/` and the
output style; the file joins that list, written idempotently the same way, so a
newly-registered project has the rules in place before it has any suites. A file
that exists only in this repo would teach nobody.

It is explicitly NOT counted as a defense. It is prose, and prose is the layer
this task's own description records as having failed — read, understood,
paraphrased into "not required", and broken. It also only reaches Claude Code
(E-1962), so it does nothing for a downstream project on another harness. The
enforcement is the runner refusal and E-1916's hook; this file explains them.

## 5. Documentation

`docs/guide/orchestration.md` "One suite per task" and "The one-command handoff
contract" both name direct invocation of the old path. Change the handoff to:

    just verify

This is the point of routing through the runner: the command a session hands back
is identical whether the suite is a script today or a manifest later, so the
handoff contract never needs rewriting again.

### `just verify [E-NNNN]` resolves its id the way `just land` does

The id is accepted but not required, using `just land`'s existing chain so the
two verbs behave alike and neither needs explaining twice:

1. an explicit argument;
2. else `endless-go tmux active-id`, the DB-backed source, which works from any
   cwd as long as the pane's session holds a task;
3. else the cwd path pattern for a task worktree, the cheap fallback outside
   tmux;
4. else a usage error naming `just verify [E-NNNN]`.

Echo the derived id, as `land` does — a verb that picks a target silently is the
same class of problem as a listing that truncates silently.

Today's recipe forwards an empty argument and lets the Python wrapper fall back
to the session's active task. That covers case 2 only: it has no cwd fallback and
says nothing about what it chose. Move the resolution into the recipe so the
chain is shared with `land` rather than a second, thinner one.

The recipe does what `esu` was doing by hand. Having resolved the task it cds
into that task's worktree and runs the suite through the WORKTREE's endless, so a
pre-land gate exercises candidate code rather than main's — the reason `esu` was
in the handoff at all. It does not need to export anything into the caller's
shell, which is the only part of `esu` a recipe cannot do and the only part this
does not need. So the documented handoff is one word:

    just verify

with the explicit `just verify E-NNNN` reserved for running a suite from
somewhere else.

**Scope note (Mike, at planning time):** `just` is the endless-dev ergonomic
wrapper, not the product surface — a downstream project has no justfile. The
shipped verb is `endless task verify`, and everything in sections 2 through 4
lives there; the recipe only resolves an id and picks a directory. Making the
product's own runner sufficient for a downstream user is deliberately deferred
until there are users to shape it around, and is NOT in this task.

Also correct the guide's claim that a suite "builds its own isolated environment"
— under the runner that is now provided, and a suite that additionally builds its
own is belt-and-braces rather than the requirement.

## Boundaries

- Does NOT port scripts to `verify.toml` (ED-1534). The move is a relocation and
  a rename, not a conversion.
- Does NOT bulk-retrofit the existing scripts to source `_harness.sh` (ED-1534).
  The guide's "don't edit a landed suite" rule is not the reason: that rule
  governs ordinary work, not an explicit restructuring of the suites themselves,
  which is what this task is. The reason is ED-1534's — churn with little value
  across ~200 land-time artifacts.
- Does NOT implement E-1916's hook. That task stands; this one does not block it
  and is not blocked by it. Either alone is an improvement; together the hook
  refuses early with a teachable message and the runner refuses structurally.
- Does NOT perform E-1623's land-time-corpus audit. E-1623 is declined: buckets
  1a and 2 were conversion scaffolding and die with the port, and buckets 1b/3
  do not justify reading 200 scripts on their own. A specific coverage gap gets
  filed on its own evidence when it surfaces.

## Risks worth naming

**Isolation changes behaviour.** Running an existing script under the runner's
isolation means `--db main` inside it resolves to the temp home's empty database.
Any script that silently depended on the real database will behave differently.
That dependency already violates the documented contract (a suite "never touches
your real config or the main database"), so a break is a finding, not a
regression — but pick the exemplar conversions to surface it early rather than
late.

**The move is the largest mechanical step.** ~200 `git mv`s plus a directory per
task. Do it as its own commit, separate from the runner change, so a bisect can
tell a relocation problem from a behaviour problem.

## PRODUCT

Nothing here is Endless-specific. Any project using Endless accumulates per-task
suites that look like a regression suite and rot. The layout, the front door, the
refusal and the marker all belong in shipped scaffolding, and the
worktree-to-task lookup is the same call in `self_dev` and downstream modes. The
CLAUDE.md is the one piece that does not travel — a downstream project on another
harness still gets the refusal, just not the explanation in that form.

## Verify — `.endless/tasks/e-2023/verify.sh`

1. Fail-fast unit gate: the Go tests this task adds to `internal/verifycmd` and
   `internal/verify`.
2. Every script moved: nothing remains under the old path, each task directory
   holds its `verify.sh`, and `git log --follow` on a sample still reaches its
   pre-move history.
3. A task with a manifest still verifies exactly as before (no regression on
   E-1603 / E-1758), and a task holding BOTH forms resolves deterministically to
   the documented one.
4. A task with only a script verifies through `just verify E-<id>`, and its
   pass/fail and exit code match running that script directly before the move.
5. A task with neither names BOTH filenames in its error.
6. The refusal fires: a landed, non-active task's suite is refused with non-zero
   exit, whichever form it takes; the session's own active task is not refused;
   bare `endless task verify` is not refused.
7. The marker works: an exemplar sourcing `_harness.sh` passes under the runner
   and refuses a bare direct run, naming `just verify`.
8. The glob shape that caused E-2071 is unreachable: iterating the suite
   directory and executing what it finds refuses at the first landed foreign
   suite.
9. `_harness.sh` sitting beside the per-task directories does not confuse
   discovery, and is not itself discoverable as a task.
10. `_harness.sh` emits TAP, and a converted exemplar's pass/fail is identical
    before and after conversion.
11. `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md` exists and the refusal messages reference it.
12. `just verify` with no argument resolves the same task `just land` would from
    the same shell, echoes what it derived, runs from inside that task's
    worktree against the worktree's own endless, and errors with a usage line
    when neither the session nor the cwd yields one.
13. THE REGRESSION THIS MUST NEVER CAUSE: a task that has landed, been reopened,
    and re-claimed verifies successfully from its own worktree — by id and with
    no id. A predicate that refuses it is wrong however elegant.
14. A freshly registered project has `.endless/tasks/CLAUDE.md` on disk, and
    re-running registration neither duplicates nor overwrites a customized one.

# Amendment — after review (Mike, 2026-08-30)

Four corrections to the plan above. Each replaces a deferral with the work, so
read the sections they name as superseded, not as history.

## A. Every suite sources the harness. No corpus is left directly runnable.

§3 and **Boundaries** deferred the retrofit, citing ED-1534's churn argument:
new suites would source `_harness.sh`, the ~200 landed ones would not, and for
those the only guard would be the runner and E-1916's hook.

That is wrong, and the plan's own thesis says why. "The enforcement point moved
from 200 places to one" is only true if the 200 cannot still be reached
individually — and `./verify.sh` reaches every one of them, skipping the
isolation and the own-task-only refusal both.

The retrofit is one line per file, inserted as the FIRST executable statement:

    source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../_harness.sh"

Placing it first is what makes it both safe and provable. Safe, because every
definition below it overrides the harness's own, so a suite written before the
harness existed behaves exactly as it did. Provable, because a direct run now
refuses before the script's own code exists — so all 202 can be executed
directly, as a test, without any of them doing anything.

ED-1534's churn argument survives where it was actually aimed: the suites are
still NOT converted to use the harness's helpers, and still not ported to
`verify.toml`. Sourcing is not conversion.

## B. The suites' own headers name the runner.

The moved scripts told the reader to run `esu && ./tests/tasks/e-NNNN-verify.sh`
— a path that no longer exists and an invocation that is now refused. Leaving
that in place under "don't edit a landed suite" gets the rule backwards: the
rule protects a suite's ASSERTIONS from being retrofitted to later code. Fixing
a comment that instructs the next reader to call it incorrectly is the opposite
of that. Every suite's header now names `endless task verify E-NNNN`; comment
lines only, no code touched.

## C. The guide documents `endless task verify`, and it is now sufficient.

§5 said the documented handoff becomes `just verify`. It cannot: `docs/guide/`
is product documentation rendered by `endless guide`, and a downstream project
has no justfile. The scope note's own reading — "the shipped verb is
`endless task verify`" — governs.

But naming a verb that could not actually do the job would teach every later
session the wrong command, so the verb was made sufficient rather than the
documentation made aspirational. `endless task verify` now:

- resolves the task from the session, falling back to the task whose worktree
  cwd is inside — `just land`'s two sources, and the second needs no database,
  so a bare call works outside tmux and in a self-dev worktree with no `--db`;
- runs the suite IN that task's worktree, because a suite proves the candidate
  tree and asking from main would otherwise run main's copy.

What is left in `just verify` is one self-dev-only thing: `--db sandbox`, which
selects the worktree's `endless-go` so the pre-land gate exercises the candidate
runner. A downstream user needs none of it. If `endless verify` is later
promoted to a top-level verb, that is a rename of a verb that already works, not
a capability gap.

## D. E-2092's finding is folded in, not filed.

Filed as a separate task, then withdrawn per ED-1550 (several symptoms of one
cause are one task; filing is the exception). The runner now exports
`ENDLESS_VERIFY_DIR` — the suite's own directory — to BOTH suite forms, so a
manifest check reads `$ENDLESS_VERIFY_DIR/e2e.sh` instead of retyping a path
whose casing has to match a convention it cannot see. `.endless/tasks/e-1603/`
is corrected to use it; the suite asserts no manifest hand-writes its own
directory again.

## Verify — additions

15. Every suite in the corpus refuses a direct run, and refuses it before
    executing a single one of its own checks.
16. `$ENDLESS_VERIFY_DIR` reaches both suite forms, and no manifest
    hand-writes its own directory.
17. `endless task verify` resolves its task from session or cwd, and runs in
    that task's worktree.

# Amendment 2 — the isolation's own artifact (2026-08-31)

Absorbed from E-2094, which is declined against the commit that implements this.
It was filed by another session as a test bug; it is this task's bug, and the
fix is one line in the runner.

## What this task did to cause it

The runner's per-run temp HOME predates this task (E-1603). What this task
changed is WHO runs under it: ~200 script suites that previously executed
directly, with the developer's real HOME, now go through the front door. On
macOS `os.MkdirTemp` lands beneath a symlinked prefix, so every one of them now
runs under a HOME reached through a symlink — which a real home directory almost
never is.

`TestProjectPath_TildeExpandsToHome` compares a resolved path against
`filepath.Join(os.UserHomeDir(), ...)`. Those agree only when HOME is not itself
symlinked, so the test had always passed and the mismatch had never shown. Any
suite whose fail-fast gate runs the monitor package now fails, reporting a
failure that has nothing to do with the task being verified.

## Why the fix is the runner's, not the test's

The plan's own risk section says "a break is a finding, not a regression" — but
that was written about suites secretly depending on the real database, where the
dependency was always a contract violation. It does not transfer:

1. The symlink is an artifact of the isolation MECHANISM, not a property of the
   system under test. The runner's job is to substitute HOME transparently;
   anything else it changes is noise it injected.
2. It is platform-dependent. The same suite passes on Linux and fails on macOS.
   A runner whose verdict depends on the OS's mktemp implementation emits false
   signal.
3. It misattributes failures — E-2094's own sharpest line, that "the failure it
   reports will point at the wrong task". That is precisely the harm this front
   door exists to prevent. Having built a gate that refuses another task's
   suite, shipping one that fails suites for reasons outside their task is the
   same error wearing different clothes.

Nothing in the contract says a suite must tolerate a symlinked HOME, and the
runner is not a fuzzer. A deliberate test of symlinked-HOME behaviour is
something someone can write on purpose.

## The change

`filepath.EvalSymlinks` on the freshly created run dir in `makeRunDir`, failing
open — a directory this process just made should always resolve, and running
under the unresolved path beats refusing to verify.

Measured: the whole `internal/monitor` package fails under a raw temp HOME with
that one test, and passes under a resolved one. So E-2094's planned per-test fix
AND its sweep for other HOME-sensitive tests both find nothing left to do.

## Why it was missed the first time

The plan said where to look — "Isolation changes behaviour ... pick the exemplar
conversions to surface it early rather than late." The exemplars chosen were
this task's own suite plus synthetic fixtures, and no pre-existing suite was
ever run under the runner. The reason was real (the new guard refuses landed
foreign suites), but the conclusion should have been "then this class cannot be
surfaced by running suites, so reason about the environment being handed to
them" — and it was not.

This task's own fail-fast gate does run `go test` under the temp HOME, but
scoped to `./internal/verify/...`, `./internal/verifycmd/...` and two named
monitor tests. One more package in that gate would have caught it. The gate was
narrowed to what this task changed, when the whole point of the change was that
OTHER tasks' gates would now run in this environment.

## Verify — additions

18. The run dir is canonical, and so are the HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME values a
    suite actually sees.
19. End to end through the real runner: a suite that observes a non-canonical
    HOME fails. Pinned as a test because the invariant is invisible on Linux and
    would otherwise rot silently.

payload.title: Surface worktree drift continuously instead of relying on someone remembering to sweep
payload.description: `endless worktree sync` reports and closes worktree drift, but only when a person runs it. Nothing surfaces that a worktree is behind, so a change to a file every task shares reaches main and reaches no working checkout until someone thinks to sweep — which is how 138 of 142 worktrees came to predate a guard they all depend on. There is also no way to watch a sweep's progress or be told when the fleet is current. Make the drift visible where a session already looks (session status, worktree list, or the handoff), and give the sweep a progress and completion signal rather than a one-shot console dump.

# Fresh evidence for part 2, the message's advice ordering (2026-08-31, ES-1159)

Filing content for E-2094, `task update --description` was refused for a genuine
absolute path — an illustrative macOS temp prefix quoted inside an explanation
OF that prefix. The gate was correct; part 1 of this task does not apply.

Part 2 does, and it cost a turn. The message ends:

    Put real content inline, or author scratch under .endless/tmp/ and load it
    with --description-file; a cross-project file can be referenced by a Git
    URL. To keep this path, add --allow-path with a regex matching it.

I read the whole message and still rephrased the prose to remove the paths,
because rephrasing is the first remedy offered and --allow-path is the last
clause of the last sentence. Mike's reaction: "you flabbergast me by avoiding
--allow-path; I asked for --allow-path precisely so you would not have to
rephrase."

So the ordering does not merely bury the flag — it actively selects against it.
An agent takes the first sanctioned option it is given, and here that option
distorts the content to satisfy the check, which is the opposite of what the
gate is for. Leading with --allow-path, as this task already proposes, would
have produced the right behaviour with no judgement required.

Second observation for the same part: the message recommends --description-file
for a DESCRIPTION. Descriptions are single-line and capped at 1024 characters,
so that advice cannot help — and following it produced a second refusal
("Description must be a single line") on the next attempt.
